facts: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) announced Thursday via a post on X that he will challenge Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for the Senate majority leader post.
Schumer, 75, has led Senate Democrats since 2017 and has served in the Senate since 1999; Van Hollen, 67, has served in the Senate since 2017 after more than a decade in the House.
The challenge comes as Democrats prepare to take control of both the House and Senate on Jan. 4, following sweeping midterm election wins earlier this month.
The Senate Democratic leadership vote will be decided by secret ballot in early December.
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) have publicly endorsed Van Hollen; Sens. Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.) and Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) have publicly backed Schumer.
Schumer says he has 'the votes' to remain leader, and his allies predict he will receive more than 40 votes in a caucus of at least 55 members.
Sens. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) and Andy Kim (D-N.J.) have both said eliminating the Senate's 60-vote filibuster threshold is under discussion as Democrats prepare to take the majority.

ladder.analysis:
The leadership fight is the first major test of how Senate Democrats plan to use the power they won in this month's midterms. Schumer has led the caucus for nearly a decade, through both majority and minority status, while Van Hollen is positioning himself as a generational and ideological break from the party establishment, campaigning on anti-special-interest themes similar to those used by successful midterm candidates. The vote, held by secret ballot in early December, will determine not just who leads the chamber but how aggressively the incoming majority approaches institutional rules, campaign-finance ties to groups like AIPAC, and strategy toward the Trump administration.

Running alongside the leadership contest is a live debate inside the Democratic caucus over whether to eliminate the legislative filibuster, the procedural rule requiring 60 votes to advance most bills. Because that threshold has historically empowered the minority party to block legislation, ending it would let Democrats pass bills with a simple majority — but would also hand the same power to Republicans whenever they next hold the chamber.
ladder.steelman: Both the leadership race and the filibuster debate turn on the same underlying tension: Democrats must decide whether to prioritize long-term institutional norms and caucus unity or short-term legislative power, knowing any rule change or leadership shift they make can just as easily be used against them when control of the Senate eventually shifts back.
ladder.implications: The outcome of the early-December secret ballot will shape not only who leads Senate Democrats starting Jan. 4 but also the caucus's appetite for structural changes like eliminating the filibuster, with consequences that could extend well beyond the current majority if Republicans later regain control.

ladder.analysis: Alaska's governorship flipped parties for the first time in more than two decades, ending a run of Republican control that began after Tony Knowles left office in 2002. The race was shaped by the state's ranked-choice voting system, which let three Republicans compete simultaneously in the general election rather than narrowing to a single GOP nominee through a primary runoff. That structure became a flashpoint when President Trump endorsed one Republican, Bernadette Wilson, while criticizing the other two for splitting conservative support. Kreiss-Tomkins, who campaigned as a bipartisan 'man of the middle' and secured cross-party endorsements, won amid voter frustration over school funding shortfalls, rising living costs, a looming natural gas shortage, and sustained outmigration from the state.
ladder.steelman: The outcome hinged as much on Alaska's unique ranked-choice system and a three-way Republican split as on any broad ideological shift, meaning the result reflects structural and candidate-specific dynamics as much as a change in the state's underlying partisan lean.
ladder.implications: Kreiss-Tomkins will need to build a mixed-party administration to govern a state facing acute fiscal and demographic pressures, including school funding gaps, high living costs, and an impending energy supply crunch. The failed repeal effort ensures ranked-choice voting will continue to shape future Alaska elections, including how multi-candidate fields from the same party compete.

stories.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi to hold historic joint meeting at APEC summit in China
body: US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping are planning to hold a historic trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, next week, the White House has confirmed. The summit runs from November 18-19. White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said Trump would arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday and that the trilateral meeting would conclude his visit to China. Trump will also hold bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday, their fourth meeting since he returned to office in 2025.

The White House said the talks would focus on reducing nuclear weapons, which Trump believes is very dangerous. A senior US official told news agencies that no agreement was expected to follow the discussions. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's largest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails. Trump has insisted on a new framework that includes China, which is rapidly building up its arsenal. Beijing has said it would be 'neither fair, reasonable nor realistic' to ask China to join trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage.

Iran is also expected to be discussed. The US and Israel launched a war on Iran on February 28; full-scale strikes have ceased but the conflict remains deadlocked. The Strait of Hormuz remains closed, affecting oil and gas prices and disrupting Chinese crude oil supplies and exports. Russia has profited from rising energy prices and recent US sanctions relief. Ukraine, however, is unlikely to be raised. A US official said Washington is pursuing peace talks through separate channels and that China is not part of that track. Trump has accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war and has lifted oil sanctions on Moscow while agreeing to allow Russian diesel into global markets.

Russia has confirmed the meeting; China has not yet officially commented on the trilateral talks, though Chinese state media reported Xi would take part in bilateral meetings at the summit. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov earlier said there were 'signals confirming readiness' for such talks. Analysts suggest the meeting may be largely performative, allowing Putin to project power and sideline the Ukraine conflict, while Trump can present himself as a global statesman. The meeting comes after Trump's Republican Party suffered a crushing defeat in midterm elections, which could weaken his leverage. Some Russian officials have drawn parallels to the 1945 Yalta conference, but Peskov said any agreements reached cannot be imposed on other nations.

stories.headline: US floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for NATO membership, Zelensky says
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday that United States negotiators raised the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership, marking the first time the proposal had been put forward. The suggestion came during the latest round of US-mediated peace talks in Abu Dhabi this week, following meetings between US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff with both Zelensky in Dublin and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. Zelensky said the question made him believe "NATO is back on the agenda," but cautioned that "you have also heard Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."

Zelensky stated that Ukraine would not cede territory, but added that if Kyiv received a comprehensive proposal including firm security guarantees, no constraints on its military, and funds for reconstruction, he would put the question to a public referendum. "The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky told reporters. The Donbas, comprising Ukraine's Donetsk and Luhansk regions, is largely occupied by Russian forces, with Russia having declared its annexation in 2022 after launching its full-scale invasion. Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donbas.

Moscow has long opposed Ukraine joining NATO, demanding instead Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality, limits on the size of Ukraine's military, and territorial concessions. Russia has also revived earlier demands for NATO to halt any expansion in its vicinity and roll back military infrastructure from central and eastern European member states. Zelensky warned that Moscow's bid to review the continent's security architecture was "dangerous because … it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations," adding that "real security in Europe means the EU and NATO."

The talks come amid strained relations between Kyiv and Washington. Trump had asked Ukraine to pause strikes on Russian oil facilities to ease global fuel prices, and Zelensky accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service, which it uses to coordinate defensive operations. Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections, which are suspended under martial law. Zelensky has said he would be willing to hold elections within months of a peace deal and would give up the presidency in exchange for NATO membership.

European representatives, including from Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Poland, are set to take part in the next round of talks, despite Moscow's longstanding insistence that European states be excluded because they support Ukraine. Meanwhile, fighting continues: Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces captured the settlement of Tersianka in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, and a Ukrainian drone attack killed three people, including a 24-month-old child, in Russia's Belgorod region. Russia launched 96 drones overnight, of which Ukraine said 81 were shot down or suppressed, while Russia claimed it intercepted 29 Ukrainian drones. Zelensky warned that Putin was "betting everything" on this winter's campaign, which Kyiv says is aimed at hurting public morale.

stories.headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid scandal; interim CEO inherits legal mess
body: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday after reports emerged of his affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative and two employees, drawing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers, the company’s board and shareholders. The company named its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO and appointed its first-ever board chair, venture investor Harvey Jones. Analysts warned that Nvidia’s value could decline 25 to 30 percent without Huang, who cofounded the AI chipmaker in 1993 and dominated its corporate structure, with dozens of executives reporting directly to him.

The scandal has ensnared the Trump administration. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s department for failing to impose export restrictions on certain Nvidia chips to China and for a delay in blacklisting Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company associated with the alleged spy that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips. White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be fired, and he is scheduled to testify before Congress next month. Senator John Cornyn said there needed to be “a thorough investigation and accountability,” adding “Heads should roll.” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer questioned what President Donald Trump knew when he invited Huang aboard Air Force One earlier this year, and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries demanded a classified briefing for all members of Congress about Nvidia.

Huang owns about 3.6 percent of Nvidia and does not have majority voting power, unlike founders of other tech giants such as Meta and Alphabet who have special stock arrangements that give them outsized control. Under Nvidia’s bylaws, Huang could be removed by the 11-person board “with or without cause.” His resignation came after Trump called him two days earlier and urged him to fight for his job, according to the New York Times.

The departure of a founder has historically hurt companies, as seen when Steve Jobs left Apple in the 1980s and the company nearly went bankrupt, and when Howard Schultz stepped down from Starbucks, which lost more than 80 percent of its value. However, some companies have thrived after founder departures: Apple continued to grow under Tim Cook, and Microsoft’s market capitalization rose from about $302 billion in 2014 to $3.88 trillion under Satya Nadella. Nvidia’s situation is complicated by the fact that much of the AI sector’s growth is pegged to its chips; OpenAI has up to $100 billion in planned financial agreements with Nvidia, and Nvidia recently agreed to invest $10 billion in Anthropic through a private placement tied to its planned IPO.

Lutnick has agreed to appear voluntarily before the Senate banking committee, and Jensen Huang is expected to answer lawmakers’ questions on Capitol Hill next month. The Senate banking committee chair, Republican Tim Scott, sent letters asking both Lutnick and Huang to appear before him, citing “serious concerns about our national security.” The developments mark a major overhaul of Nvidia’s corporate structure and leadership as the company, valued at nearly $4 trillion, navigates the fallout from the scandal.

stories.headline: US shifts to economic pressure as Iran war stalemate continues; Iran claims strike on US radar in Bahrain
body: The United States is pivoting to economic pressure on Iran as the war that began on February 28 remains at a stalemate, with President Donald Trump sidelining Vice President JD Vance from the Iran file and declaring a deal is no longer a priority. Iran claimed its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps struck a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday, but the US military's Central Command denied the claim and said it shot down two Iranian attack drones with no casualties or damage. Tehran said the strike was retaliation for a US attack on a telecommunications tower in Iran's Sirik county on the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump wrote on Truth Social that "we don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money." Vance, who had been the US chief negotiator and favored a negotiated resolution, was redirected to focus on alleged Democratic corruption after Republicans lost their House majority in midterm elections, losses Vance blamed on the unpopular war. Mediated contacts via Qatar continue but no breakthrough is expected; Tehran demands seven conditions and clear sequencing of concessions, which Washington finds unacceptable. Professor Nasser Hadian of the University of Tehran said Vance's sidelining signals that reaching a deal is not a priority and that the US believes economic pressure can force concessions.

The war has severely disrupted the Strait of Hormuz, a critical transit point for global oil and gas supplies. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations recorded 139 outbound and 169 inbound transits in the past week, approximately 65 percent below pre-conflict levels. Iran continues to attack ships it considers unauthorized users of the waterway, while the US Navy enforces a blockade of Iranian vessels and escorts tankers. The International Monetary Fund says Gulf Arab states are in economic recession despite higher oil prices: Kuwait, Qatar and Iraq are contracting approximately 16 percent this year; Bahrain's economy is down 11 percent.

Trump met Qatar's prime minister this week and said afterward that Gulf Arab allies prefer "the status quo" of continued economic pressure on Iran. He wrote that while the US remains "locked and loaded," an attack "seems to be quite unlikely." However, the US is sending a third aircraft carrier with thousands of troops to the region, keeping open the possibility of escalation. Iranian media said the US struck one of Iran's islands in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday. Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at an APEC summit in China next week to discuss ending the war. Senior UAE diplomat Anwar Gargash said the region must "prepare for a prolonged period of uncertainty."

stories.headline: Commerce Secretary Lutnick ties to Nvidia scrutinized as Bessent blames chip leakage
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department and others in the Trump administration had long supported restricting Megaspeed, the company at the center of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's spy-sex scandal, but that the Commerce Department is in charge of the entity list. 'You will have to ask them about their internal processes,' Bessent told CNBC's 'Squawk Box,' pointing to Secretary Howard Lutnick's department as the one responsible for imposing the sanctions. The remarks came as new scrutiny fell on Lutnick's ties to Nvidia following Axios reports that he repeatedly resisted a crackdown on companies suspected of funneling Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, despite President Donald Trump authorizing new export restrictions.

A CNBC analysis of securities filings found that Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm formerly run by Lutnick and now led by his sons Brandon and Kyle, reduced its reported Nvidia holdings by 49% between September 2025 and March 2026, from 3.5 million shares to 1.78 million, as the value fell from $652 million to $310 million. The decline coincided with U.S. intelligence warnings about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy and pressure on Lutnick to crack down on Megaspeed. Cantor said its 13F filings reflect client swap transactions and that its proprietary positions in Nvidia are 'only immaterial.' The firm declined further comment. There is no evidence Lutnick shared nonpublic information with his sons, ethics experts said, though Richard Painter, former White House ethics lawyer, noted 'the appearance doesn't look great.'

Even as Cantor pared its Nvidia stake, it maintained deep business ties to the company's AI empire. In May 2025, Cantor served as one of seven bookrunners on a $3 billion convertible bond offering for IREN, an Australian cloud computing provider that had just signed a $3.4 billion contract with Nvidia. By June 2026, Cantor reported $115 million in IREN shares and $362 million in Nvidia shares. Earlier, in October 2025, Cantor advised AI infrastructure developer Lancium on a $600 million financing deal for a Stargate data center campus; Nvidia later invested $2 billion for a roughly 20% stake in Lancium. Cantor also has ties to Nvidia's supply chain: Semafor reported in May 2025 that Cantor bankers informally advised TSMC on navigating Washington, which Cantor called 'baseless and false.'

The scrutiny intensified after Huang's resignation Thursday and amid reporting that Lutnick had received a classified intelligence memo in May 2025 about Huang's relationship with a suspected spy, yet appeared alongside Huang at a G20 technology summit and later cleared roughly 10 Chinese companies, including Alibaba and ByteDance, to buy Nvidia's H200 chips. Sens. Jim Banks and Elizabeth Warren in March urged Lutnick to reconsider Nvidia's export licenses after indictments in a chip-smuggling case. On Wednesday, Sens. Warren and Chris Coons demanded that Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller preserve records on Nvidia chip exports and intelligence warnings. Coons told CNBC on Friday that the administration 'has most failed here in being persuaded by Jensen Huang and others to license the export of some advanced chips.'

The White House has expressed 'complete confidence' in Lutnick, and a White House official told Reuters on Thursday that Trump is standing by the commerce secretary. Cantor's next quarterly securities filing is due Monday, which will show whether its Nvidia holdings continued at lower levels. The episode raises questions about the intersection of Lutnick's family financial interests and his role overseeing export controls at Commerce, though no evidence of wrongdoing has emerged. Painter cautioned that 'the Trump administration leaks like a sieve when it comes to nonpublic government information,' but stressed there is no proof Lutnick shared such information with his sons.

stories.headline: Warsh Plan to Remake Fed: Fewer Rate Votes, More Deliberation; 2027 Calendar Confirmed
body: The Federal Reserve on Thursday released its 2027 meeting schedule, confirming that the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will hold eight meetings but vote on interest rates at only seven of them. The October 26-27 gathering will be dedicated to "broad monetary policy strategy issues," the Fed said, marking the first time a scheduled meeting will not include a rate decision [thehill.com](https://thehill.com/business/6219883-fed-announces-2027-meeting-schedule/). The change, announced last month by Chair Kevin Warsh, reduces the number of rate-setting meetings from the long-standing eight per year to seven [nhk.or.jp](https://www3.nhk.or.jp/nhkworld/news/20261113de75679/).

Under the new calendar, the final rate-setting meeting of 2027 will be held November 16-17, replacing a previously scheduled December 7-8 meeting. After that, the FOMC will not meet again until January 25-26, 2028, creating a two-month gap that Warsh said would allow more economic data to accumulate between meetings [investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/fed-sets-new-meeting-schedule-for-2027-as-foretold-by-warsh-5023024). Warsh has said he expects the committee to hold two strategy-only meetings and six rate-setting meetings in 2028 [thehill.com](https://thehill.com/business/6219883-fed-announces-2027-meeting-schedule/).

Warsh first floated the schedule change during the FOMC's July meeting, according to minutes, arguing that six meetings per year held every two months would "allow more information to accumulate between meetings" [thehill.com](https://thehill.com/business/6219883-fed-announces-2027-meeting-schedule/). He formally announced the plan last month after the committee held interest rates steady at a range of 3.75% to 4%. "Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals," Warsh told reporters. "But it's equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations — for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point" [thehill.com](https://thehill.com/business/6219883-fed-announces-2027-meeting-schedule/).

The schedule change is the latest example of Warsh putting his imprint on the central bank since succeeding Jerome Powell in May. He has also declined to submit his own "dot" projections in the FOMC's quarterly economic outlook, making him the only one of the 19 committee members not to do so. Warsh has said market participants "are learning to play the ball, not the referee" without such forward guidance [thehill.com](https://thehill.com/business/6219883-fed-announces-2027-meeting-schedule/). He has established a task force to review the Fed's communications practices, including whether to continue publishing the dot plot. The Fed's updated meeting page no longer marks the March, June, and September 2027 meetings with an asterisk indicating they are gatherings for quarterly economic projections, a practice Warsh has been disdainful of since it began under former Chair Ben Bernanke [investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/fed-sets-new-meeting-schedule-for-2027-as-foretold-by-warsh-5023024).

The move drew praise from Jason Furman, who chaired the Council of Economic Advisers under President Barack Obama. "I have long thought the Fed spends too much time on the immediate and not nearly enough time thinking about longer-term strategy," Furman wrote on X, calling the change a "great move" [thehill.com](https://thehill.com/business/6219883-fed-announces-2027-meeting-schedule/). Under the Federal Reserve Act, the FOMC is required to meet at least four times per year [thehill.com](https://thehill.com/business/6219883-fed-announces-2027-meeting-schedule/).

stories.headline: FAA lifts rare nationwide ground stop; airline stocks fall
body: The Federal Aviation Administration lifted a rare nationwide ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday after aging infrastructure forced the agency to halt all outbound flights for hours, stranding passengers at airports across the United States. The ground stop, ordered around 5 p.m. Eastern, came after the FAA reported a temporary telecommunications outage and said it acted "out of an abundance of caution." At the time, roughly 3,500 planes were in the air, but more than 10,000 flights were disrupted.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a press conference that aging infrastructure caused the outage. "Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data, and they went down…and I shouldn't say they went down. They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers, and because of that, we shut the system down," he said. Duffy added that the system needs a complete overhaul, including investment in new towers and airports, which he estimated would cost about $50 billion.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there is "zero evidence" of a cyberattack. Meanwhile, Microsoft said in a statement on X that the FAA ground stop was not related to any of its services, after the tech giant apologized earlier Friday for a separate software outage that left users unable to access Outlook email and other services.

Airline stocks fell in post-market trading Friday on the news. Shares of American Airlines, Southwest, JetBlue, Delta Air Lines, and United Airlines all moved lower. The economic impact of the outage remains unknown. High jet-fuel costs mean fewer flights are available for travelers seeking to rebook, and delays are expected to extend into the weekend, with the FAA planning to prioritize aircraft carrying more passengers.

This nationwide grounding was extremely rare. The last time the FAA halted all U.S. departures was in January 2023 due to a system outage. Prior to that, traffic was halted after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

stories.headline: Dejounte Murray Requests Trade from Pelicans; Suns, Heat, Bucks Emerge as Potential Destinations
body: New Orleans Pelicans point guard Dejounte Murray has requested a trade, the team confirmed Friday, with agent Rich Paul working alongside team officials on a resolution. ESPN’s Shams Charania first reported the request. The Pelicans said in a statement that they "will evaluate potential trade opportunities that are in the best interest of our organization." Murray was ruled out for Friday night’s NBA Cup game against the Memphis Grizzlies, which the Pelicans lost 142-111 to fall to 4-9.

Murray, 30, is averaging 13.4 points, 4.6 rebounds, 4.4 assists and 1.6 steals this season. He started the season with averages of 17.8 points, 5.8 rebounds and 6.0 assists in four October games, but his numbers have dropped sharply; in his last five games he has averaged 10.0 points, 3.6 rebounds and 3.2 assists, missing the 10-point mark three times. Murray is trying to regain form after being limited to 14 games last season due to an Achilles injury, which he called his "worst experience in the NBA" during an appearance on The Pivot last year. He also recently defended himself from fans blaming him for the team’s struggles in deleted social media posts.

According to NBA insider Chris Haynes, the Phoenix Suns "have registered interest" in Murray. The Athletic’s Sam Amick reported that Murray has a "strong interest" in going to Phoenix and that his camp has been hopeful a deal would materialize in which he would be swapped for Suns guard Jalen Green. Amick added that team sources on both sides recently insisted there had not been any talks about that deal, but that "certainly could change." ClutchPoints’ Brett Siegel also reported that the Pelicans could call the Suns about a possible deal. The Athletic’s Sam Amick earlier reported that opposing clubs feel the Suns are "motivated" to trade Green for a proven point guard.

Other potential landing spots include the Miami Heat and the Milwaukee Bucks, per Haynes. ESPN’s Bobby Marks explained the salary cap implications of a Murray trade. The Heat could benefit from having another setup man for Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo, which would relieve Davion Mitchell of ball-handling duties and move veteran sharpshooter Klay Thompson to a sixth-man role. The Bucks recently benched Ryan Rollins to start rookie Brayden Burries alongside Tyler Herro, but the youngster has struggled to find his footing. The Pelicans are already prepared to hand the reins to second-year point guard Jeremiah Fears, making a trade likely sooner rather than later.

Green, in his second season in Phoenix, is averaging 11.8 points, 3.4 rebounds and 3.1 assists, with his numbers regressing from his rookie campaign. Both players could benefit from a change of scenery, and a potential swap between the Pelicans and Suns is a situation to monitor. Murray’s trade request comes after he posted on X following a loss to the Brooklyn Nets on Wednesday, making a bold allegation about the team that sources described as the last straw for the guard, who is unhappy with his role.

stories.headline: Amanda Nunes and Kayla Harrison set for UFC 334 showdown
body: Amanda Nunes, the most successful women's mixed martial artist of all time, returns from a three-year retirement to challenge women's bantamweight champion Kayla Harrison at UFC 334 on Saturday at Madison Square Garden in New York. The fight, originally scheduled for January, was postponed after Harrison required neck and spinal surgery. Harrison, a two-time Olympic gold medalist in judo and a two-time PFL lightweight champion, won the UFC bantamweight title in only her third fight with the promotion.

Nunes, 38, left the UFC in 2023 as a former featherweight and bantamweight champion, the only woman to hold titles in two weight classes simultaneously and the only fighter, male or female, to successfully defend both belts. She holds multiple records, including 11 wins in title fights, tied for most in women's UFC history. During her career, Nunes defeated icons such as Ronda Rousey, Cris Cyborg, and Valentina Shevchenko. She won 23 of 28 fights, with 13 knockouts.

"I'm here to stay," Nunes told CBS Sports. "I'm a fighter, man. This is a huge difference between me and Kayla. She's an athlete. I'm a fighter." Nunes insists she is not returning as a challenger. "I'm here as a double champion," she said. "I needed a break and did it at the right time for my mind, body and soul." Nunes said she was motivated to return after Harrison joined the UFC, seeing a new challenge in a division she felt she had cleaned out.

"I feel like 20, honestly. I didn't expect to feel like that," she said. "Everything is coming together perfect. The training. Everything [feels] like I never left this game." She also cited a desire to revive interest in women's MMA, which she believes has slowed since her departure. "I got upset when I left because I wanted to see the division grow," Nunes told the BBC. "I want to make women's MMA great."

Harrison, 36, described her own recovery from neck surgery as a battle leading up to the fight. She had been competing with herniated discs dating back to her judo career. The contest is being billed as one of the biggest women's fights in UFC history. Nunes enters as a betting underdog, a position she said she welcomes. "I have always been the underdog," she said. "I take that as a motivator." Nunes also expressed desire to face the team that she believes did not have her best interests at heart, as her former coaches at American Top Team will be in Harrison's corner. Nunes said she plans to fight on after Saturday "until my body tells me to stop."

stories.headline: Red Sox sign Jake Bauers to 4-year, $58 million contract; ex-Brewer to serve as primary DH
body: The Boston Red Sox signed free-agent first baseman/outfielder Jake Bauers to a four-year, $58 million contract on Friday, according to multiple outlets. The deal was first reported by ESPN’s Jeff Passan. Bauers, who turns 31, rejected a $23.15 million qualifying offer from the Milwaukee Brewers, meaning the Red Sox will forfeit their second- and fifth-highest selections in the 2027 draft and $1 million from their international bonus pool after exceeding the competitive-balance tax threshold in 2026.

Bauers is expected to serve as Boston’s primary designated hitter, with occasional starts at first base to give Willson Contreras more rest after Contreras dealt with soft-tissue injuries late last season. Contreras will remain the primary first baseman, as he grades out as a better defender. Bauers can also play left field, but the Red Sox already have Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Jarren Duran and Eli White in the outfield. The signing increases the likelihood that Boston trades Duran and appears to mark the end of Masataka Yoshida’s tenure, as Yoshida enters the final season of his five-year, $90 million contract and is a change-of-scenery candidate. Curtis Mead, who could have logged DH at-bats, is now expected to be the everyday second baseman.

Bauers enjoyed a breakout 2026 season for the World Series-champion Brewers, hitting .266 with a .389 on-base percentage, .484 slugging percentage and .874 OPS in 144 games. He set career highs with 26 home runs, 22 doubles, 86 RBIs and 93 runs, and posted a 3.6 fWAR after entering the season with a minus-0.4 career fWAR. His .389 OBP ranked third in all of baseball, and he finished in the 91st percentile or above in hard-hit rate (51.9%), bat speed (76.5 mph), expected wOBA (.371), barrel rate (14.0%), chase rate (21.7%) and walk rate (16.3%). Bauers was named MVP of the National League Championship Series after the Brewers swept the Los Angeles Dodgers. He had previously played for the Rays, Guardians, Mariners and Yankees before signing with Milwaukee before the 2025 season.

The Red Sox are gambling that Bauers’s 2026 performance was not a fluke, similar to their acquisition of Curtis Mead last July after a first-half breakout. Bauers brings October experience from three consecutive postseason trips in Milwaukee, including deep runs the past two years, and joins a Boston clubhouse that already includes Contreras, Ranger Suárez and Aroldis Chapman. The Red Sox have not won a postseason series since 2021. The deal adds to the team’s estimated luxury-tax payroll, which now sits at approximately $269 million per FanGraphs, about $3 million less than the final 2026 figure.

The timing of the signing marks an aggressive early move for Boston, which has been slower in free agency in recent years. This offseason, Bauers is the first player to sign a contract worth more than $40 million; the only other major league deals signed to this point were reliever contracts for Emilio Pagán (Detroit) and Evan Phillips (Atlanta). The Red Sox have now accepted draft-pick penalties for signing a qualified free agent for the third straight year, following Alex Bregman in 2025 and Ranger Suárez in 2026. Meanwhile, the Brewers are considering options to replace Bauers at first base, including retaining Andrew Vaughn or promoting prospects Andrew Fischer, Blake Burke or Luke Adams. They are not expected to pursue free agent Ty France, who also broke out in 2026.

stories.headline: FDA Approves Durvalumab Plus Enfortumab Vedotin for Perioperative Treatment of Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer
body: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved on November 13, 2026, the combination of durvalumab (Imfinzi) and enfortumab vedotin-ejfv (Padcev) as neoadjuvant treatment followed by adjuvant durvalumab monotherapy after radical cystectomy for adults with muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) who are ineligible for or have declined cisplatin-based chemotherapy. The decision, granted under priority review and Project Orbis, was based on interim results from the phase 3 VOLGA trial (NCT04960709), which showed a 49% reduction in the risk of an event-free survival (EFS) event (hazard ratio [HR], 0.51; 95% CI, 0.38–0.67; P < .001) and a 42% reduction in the risk of death (HR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.40–0.83; P = .003) compared with radical cystectomy alone.

In the VOLGA trial, 695 patients with clinical stage T2-T4aN0/1M0 or T1N1M0 MIBC who were candidates for cystectomy but ineligible for or refused cisplatin were randomly assigned 1:1:1 to either the approved doublet (durvalumab plus enfortumab vedotin before surgery then adjuvant durvalumab), a triplet that also included tremelimumab, or surgery alone. The median EFS for the doublet arm was not reached (95% CI, 33.2 months–not reached) versus 12.1 months (95% CI, 7.6–27.0) for surgery alone, and the 24-month EFS rates were 63.5% and 45.1%, respectively. The median overall survival was not reached in either arm, with 24-month OS rates of 78.4% (doublet) and 69.4% (surgery). Pathologic complete response was achieved in 45.1% of patients in the doublet arm versus 9.6% in the surgery arm.

The recommended dosage for patients weighing 30 kg or more is durvalumab 1500 mg every 3 weeks plus enfortumab vedotin 1.25 mg/kg on days 1 and 8 of each 21-day cycle for 3 neoadjuvant cycles, followed by durvalumab 1500 mg every 4 weeks for up to 9 cycles after surgery. For patients weighing less than 30 kg, the dose is durvalumab 20 mg/kg on the same schedules. Enfortumab vedotin is administered only in the neoadjuvant phase. The FDA’s review relied on EFS assessed by blinded independent central review.

Grade 3 or higher adverse events of any cause occurred in 71.1% of patients receiving the doublet compared with 50.2% in the surgery-alone arm. Treatment-related grade 3 or higher events were reported in 30.7% of the doublet arm, with one treatment-related death (multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome). The most common any-grade adverse events in the doublet arm included pruritus (44%), urinary tract infection (36%), and anemia (32%). Skin reactions, peripheral neuropathy, and hyperglycemia were also noted. The FDA label includes warnings for immune-mediated adverse reactions, infusion-related reactions, complications of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and embryo-fetal toxicity.

"Up to half of patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer are not eligible for cisplatin and face high rates of disease recurrence, even after having their bladder removed, leaving a significant need for new effective and well-tolerated treatments," said Thomas Powles, MD, professor and chair of Barts Cancer Centre and international coordinating investigator for VOLGA, in a news release on the survival findings. "The VOLGA results show that perioperative durvalumab significantly extends event-free survival and overall survival when combined with neoadjuvant enfortumab vedotin, with a manageable safety profile, compared to surgery for patients in this curative-intent setting."

The triplet arm (durvalumab, tremelimumab, and enfortumab vedotin) also met the EFS endpoint but did not show a statistically significant overall survival benefit at the interim analysis (HR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.54–1.07; P = .12); it is not part of the approved indication. The approval was supported by the VOLGA trial’s primary endpoint of EFS and key secondary endpoint of OS, with a median EFS follow-up of 22.9 months at the data cutoff of March 2, 2026. The FDA’s decision comes six weeks ahead of its goal date, underscoring the unmet need in this patient population.

stories.headline: FDA revokes approval of three cancer-linked chemicals in food coloring and produce inks
body: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced Monday that it will revoke authorization for the use of three chemicals — methylene chloride, ethylene dichloride, and trichloroethylene — in certain food colorings and produce inks, citing links to cancer. The decision, which takes effect Jan. 11, 2027, targets methylene chloride in inks used to mark fruits and vegetables, as well as all three chemicals in the production of turmeric oleoresin, annatto extract, and paprika oleoresin.

The revocations follow a petition from several groups — including Breast Cancer Prevention Partners, the Environmental Working Group, the Center for Environmental Health, the International Association of Color Manufacturers, and the Environmental Defense Fund — that invoked the Delaney Clause of the Federal Food, Drug & Cosmetic Act. That clause mandates that any color additive intended for ingestion must be deemed unsafe if evidence shows it causes cancer in humans or animals.

An Environmental Defense Fund press release said exposure to the three chemicals "has been linked to cancer, along with other serious health conditions like heart defects in babies and damage to the liver, kidney and immune system." However, the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry notes that it is not known if methylene chloride can cause cancer in humans, though inhaling large amounts has been linked to cancer risks in mice. The World Health Organization, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the Environmental Protection Agency have characterized the chemical as a possible human carcinogen.

In California, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who once dismissed dye bans, later authored the so-called "Skittles ban" bill. Consumer Reports delivered 100,000 signatures to the FDA over additives in snacks. A California lawsuit alleges that millions of Driscoll's berry trays exceeded Canada's pesticide limit, and a U.S. Cyclospora outbreak has drawn scrutiny to the FDA's declining foreign inspections.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang leaves Nvidia after scandals; analysts say company can survive without him
body: Jensen Huang, the co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, has left the company he led for 33 years following allegations of involvement in two chip smuggling scandals and three extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The 63-year-old visionary, who built Nvidia into a $5 trillion company representing roughly 6 percent of the S&P 500, had no named successor and around 60 employees reporting directly to him, making his departure a seismic event for the AI industry and stock market.

Huang resigned after reportedly enabling the smuggling scandals and amid the infidelity allegations, which surfaced as he mingled with President Donald Trump. He had once said he preferred to die on the job and suggested he would work until age 90 or 100, then continue as a robot. Analysts describe his leadership as singular: “Jensen is Nvidia, and Nvidia is Jensen,” said Jon Peddie, a computer industry analyst who has tracked Nvidia since its inception. “He was the consummate showman, salesman, and visionary,” added IDC analyst Tom Mainelli.

Huang’s legacy includes a series of high-stakes bets that transformed Nvidia from a PC graphics company into the dominant supplier of chips powering the AI boom. In 2006, he bet the company’s entire gross profit on CUDA, a technology that allowed GPUs to handle non-graphics tasks, despite no market demand. That bet paid off when University of Toronto researchers used Nvidia GPUs in 2012 to train AlexNet, a breakthrough image-recognition network widely credited with sparking the AI revolution. “He had the vision for what it could be and the courage to pursue it,” Peddie said.

Despite Huang’s departure, analysts do not expect an immediate business crisis. “This is a stock shock, not a business shock, for the next year,” said Pat Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy. “The roadmap and manufacturing are locked in through 2027.” Creative Strategies analyst Ben Bajarin noted that the product roadmap remains strong, with several generations already in design or on order. “The product roadmap is set and remains strong… That supply position does not walk out the door with one person,” he said.

The bigger risk, according to analysts, is longer-term strategic vision. “The question is whether Nvidia keeps inventing at Jensen’s pace once those plans run out,” Moorhead said. Huang built an exceptionally talented organization, but his departure leaves a leadership gap that may require an outsider. “No one in the company really wants to step into his shoes, so an outsider is going to have to be found,” one source noted. Nvidia’s future hinges on choosing a successor with technical credibility and a plan to protect its CUDA ecosystem, while navigating the fallout from the scandals that prompted Huang’s exit.

stories.headline: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop; officials investigate possible role of new AI system
body: The Federal Aviation Administration lifted its third-ever nationwide ground stop Friday evening, clearing domestic flights to resume takeoffs at 8:35 p.m. EST after a communications outage halted departures from all U.S. airports for more than four hours. The stoppage, which began at 3:36 p.m. EST, affected more than one million travelers, with FlightAware reporting 9,124 U.S. flights delayed and 5,901 canceled as of 8:39 p.m. ET. Some airlines, including Air Canada, canceled all flights to and from the United States for the remainder of the evening.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the disruption on an aging air traffic control system, saying in a post on X that the system relies on "DECADES-OLD analog equipment that simply cannot compete with the demands of the 21st century." In a White House press conference, Duffy said Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON) facilities "started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and the communications from airplanes," and that analog telecom switches and routers "got overloaded with data." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed that "patches" to the existing system sparked the issue, though Duffy added, "By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system… I didn’t anticipate that we would have an outage like this."

The outage began at the Chicago air traffic control center, according to The Air Current, followed by centers in Boston, Washington, New York, and Minneapolis, disrupting both radar and radio frequencies used by controllers and pilots. The FAA issued the ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety," and said inbound international flights would be managed case by case. Mullin told reporters there is no reason to suspect a cyberattack or connection to a recent Microsoft Outlook outage, but that no cause had been ruled out for the "telecommunications outage."

Officials are investigating whether the FAA’s new artificial intelligence system, the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) tool, contributed to the disruption. The system, designed by Air Space Intelligence (ASI) under a 12-year, $875 million contract awarded in June, was activated nationwide on November 10 and uses real-time data on weather, congestion, and flight paths to streamline routes. Mullin said the Department of Homeland Security is working with federal agencies to examine any connection, but stressed there is no threat to the public. ASI denied any link, posting that "the current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC."

The last nationwide ground stop occurred in 2023 and lasted about 90 minutes after the NOTAM system went down; the one before that followed the September 11, 2001 attacks. Duffy cautioned that without massive system updates, there will be "more of these" outages ahead, and said he is pursuing funds to replace the outdated equipment. The FAA said technicians continue to investigate the communications failure affecting air traffic control centers nationwide.

stories.headline: Microsoft outage escalates into global cloud crisis, experts say worse than CrowdStrike
body: A widespread outage that began midday Thursday has disrupted Microsoft 365 services globally, affecting email, cloud storage, AI tools, and security software for hundreds of millions of users. Ciaran Martin, former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, called it 'one of the biggest outages of all time,' suggesting it may be 'worse' than the recent CrowdStrike and Amazon Web Services disruptions.

The outage struck Microsoft's Outlook email, Teams video conferencing, Copilot AI, Defender security screening, and Intune management dashboards, as well as cloud-based Windows computers. Businesses, hospitals, police departments, schools, and government agencies were affected. In Japan, deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said government IT infrastructure was disrupted. The Supreme Court in the Philippines experienced legal work delays, and a Colorado sheriff's office reported difficulty posting bonds for prisoner release. Financial transactions were blocked when users could not receive verification codes for bank transfers. Microsoft estimated in January that it has over 450 million paid commercial subscriptions.

Microsoft attributed the failure to 'a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable' and 'failed server health checks.' The company said it has 'no evidence of malicious activity' and that the incident is 'not related to cyber or AI / agents.' Recovery efforts continued into Friday, with Microsoft extending email timeout to 48 hours to preserve delayed mail. Doug Madory of Kentik noted that traffic was returning to Microsoft services after roughly 18 hours of downtime.

Microsoft's executive vice president Charles Lamanna stated Friday that 'we’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure. Our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward.' The company promised a full post-incident report with root cause analysis after mitigation is complete. The outage follows a similar dayslong cloud service disruption in September 2023, which Microsoft blamed on a 'core authentication configuration' issue.

The prolonged disruption and slow recovery have raised questions about Microsoft's ability to swiftly rebound from internal failures. While the company has ruled out malicious activity, the scope of the incident—affecting everything from hospital communications to court operations—underscores the dependence on Microsoft's cloud ecosystem and the cascading risks of a single provider's service failure.
